title: What to Do When Someone Dies in Afghanistan: 5-Step Official Checklist
titleEn: What to Do When Someone Dies in Afghanistan: 5-Step Official Checklist
cardSummary: Official 5-step bereavement checklist for Afghanistan: medical death certification, civil death registration, funeral and repatriation permits, survivor benefits, and estate succession.
introHtml: Handling legal and administrative procedures following a death in Afghanistan requires in-person local verification because, following institutional disruption and the absence of accessible functioning state web portals under de facto administration, domestic civil-registry and court websites (including the National Statistics and Information Authority portal) are offline or unreachable from abroad [1][5][8]. To provide verifiable statutory and procedural guidance despite offline domestic websites, this guide anchors rules covering the 1977 Civil Code, population registration, labour law, and disability statutes in verified international legal archives (FAOLEX, WIPO Lex, UNHCR Refworld, and ILO NATLEX) alongside foreign civil-document reciprocity and diplomatic mission pages (travel.state.gov, GOV.UK, UNHCR, and accredited Afghan diplomatic missions), advising in-person verification at local municipal or district offices or accredited diplomatic missions [1][2][3][4][6].

steps.title: Medical notification, hospital vs. rural deaths, and witness proof
steps.html:
• Urban hospitals vs. home deaths: For deaths in major cities, families request an initial medical death notice from the treating hospital under the Ministry of Public Health and Provincial Hospitals in Afghanistan; in rural districts where deaths predominantly occur at home without medical supervision, local practice relies on confirmation from community elders (Maliks or Wakil-e Guzars) and two adult witnesses [1][5][9].
  • Police and district clearance: Where a death results from accident, violence, or unexplained causes, local police or district security authorities must inspect and document the event before local clearance is issued [1][8].
  • Practical documentation caution: Because rural healthcare records are sparse, retaining hospital intake slips, two adult witness statements, and copies of any family Tazkira prevents severe delays in establishing date and cause of death [1][5].

steps.title: Civil death registration and Tazkira updates
steps.html:
• In-person civil-registry filing: Under the Law on Registration of Population Records (2014), civil registration of births, deaths, and national identity cards (Tazkira or biometric e-Tazkira) is handled locally through Municipal, District, and Provincial Civil Registration Offices (Tazkira / NSIA) [4][5].
  • Evidentiary chain for death certificates: Official death certificates typically require presenting the deceased's or close relative's Tazkira, hospital notification (if any), confirmation letters from local community leaders (Maliks or Wakils), statements from two adult witnesses, and municipal or district office verification [1][5].
  • Barriers for women and displaced families: According to UNHCR and UK Home Office civil-documentation reporting, women and displaced residents hold Tazkira documents at markedly lower rates than men and face male-chaperone (mahram) accompaniment restrictions at municipal offices, so designating a documented male next of kin or authorized representative is often necessary inside Afghanistan [5][8].

steps.title: Local burial and international repatriation considerations
steps.html:
• Prompt Islamic burial and no cremation: Under prevailing Islamic and municipal practice, burial takes place promptly in community or municipal cemeteries without public cremation facilities [1].
  • Cross-border repatriation hurdles: Repatriating remains outside Afghanistan is logistically difficult due to limited international flights, absence of standardized commercial embalming services outside major urban hospitals, and closed foreign embassies in Kabul; families must coordinate with destination-country consular authorities and medical authorities before attempting cross-border transport [1][8][9].
  • Protecting original identity papers: Families handling overseas matters should scan and safely retain the deceased's passport, paper Tazkira, and e-Tazkira before local cancellation or court filing [1][5].

steps.title: Estate settlement, Civil Code (1977), and court inheritance letters
steps.html:
• Court inheritance determination: Civil death notification does not transfer bank accounts, land deeds (Qabala), or personal property; heirs must petition Local Courts (Mahkama) and Ministry of Foreign Affairs Consular Department in Kabul under the Civil Code of the Republic of Afghanistan (1977) (Articles 1993 to 2197) for a formal Inheritance Certificate (Hasr-e Werathat) [2][3][6].
  • Islamic inheritance shares and one-third will cap: The 1977 Civil Code sets mandatory Sharia-aligned inheritance shares across spouses, children, and ascendants (ordinarily granting sons twice the share of daughters), while testamentary wills are restricted to one-third of the net estate unless adult heirs consent [2][3].
  • Powers of Attorney for overseas heirs: Heirs living abroad who cannot travel to Afghanistan can execute a Power of Attorney or Inheritance Certificate through functioning Accredited Afghan Diplomatic Missions Abroad (Consular Services); for example, the Afghan Embassy in Vienna requires an in-person appointment, two Afghan or Muslim adult male witnesses with IDs, and subsequent certification in Kabul by the Ministry of Foreign Affairs Consular Department [6][8].

steps.title: Disability/survivor claims and consular legalization (non-Apostille)
steps.html:
• Labour and disability benefits context: Statutory work-related protections under Afghanistan's Labour Law (No. 35 of 2007) and survivor/disability provisions in prior state benefit laws remain severely disrupted under de facto institutional funding limits; families with dependents carrying certified disabilities should check local status through provincial offices alongside humanitarian protection channels [7][8].
  • Non-Apostille treaty status: According to the Hague Conference on Private International Law (HCCH) status table, Afghanistan is not a Contracting Party to the 1961 Hague Apostille Convention; an Apostille stamp cannot authenticate Afghan documents or foreign records for Afghanistan [10].
  • Consular legalization path: Foreign court letters, translations, and Afghan civil certificates require sequential consular legalization involving Local Courts (Mahkama) and Ministry of Foreign Affairs Consular Department in Kabul plus Accredited Afghan Diplomatic Missions Abroad (Consular Services) and destination-country embassies where operational [1][6][10].

closingQuestion: Are you managing civil registration and court probate locally inside Afghanistan, or seeking a consular Power of Attorney through an operational mission abroad?

contacts.name: Municipal, District, and Provincial Civil Registration Offices (Tazkira / NSIA)
contacts.note: Local district and provincial offices processing Tazkira identity records and in-person civil death registration.

contacts.name: Ministry of Public Health and Provincial Hospitals in Afghanistan
contacts.note: Public hospitals and provincial clinics issuing initial medical death notifications and disease-clearance certificates.

contacts.name: Local Courts (Mahkama) and Ministry of Foreign Affairs Consular Department in Kabul
contacts.note: Judicial courts issuing Hasr-e Werathat inheritance decrees under the 1977 Civil Code and Kabul MFA department certifying consular Powers of Attorney.

contacts.name: Accredited Afghan Diplomatic Missions Abroad (Consular Services)
contacts.note: Operational Afghan embassies (such as Vienna) issuing Powers of Attorney and inheritance letters in person with two witnesses.
